newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy surged as 1996 ended but inflation muted.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy surged as 1996 ended but inflation muted.

text.p: The economy snapped back and grew at the fastest pace in 2-1/2 years in the fourth quarter, the government said Friday, as consumer spending and exports surged without firing up inflation.
The nation's gross domestic product grew at a surprisingly strong 4.7 percent annual rate in the quarter, more than double the 2.1 percent rate in the third quarter, the Commerce Department said.

Despite the pickup in growth, price rises were the smallest in 30 years as the economy showed few signs of overheating that might push the Federal Reserve into raising interest rates soon in a bid to ward off inflation.

"It's in many ways an economy that is a picture of perfection," said Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago. He said the jump in growth was unlikely to be repeated in the current quarter.
"We have an economy that is growing at a pace that is unsustainable on a long-term basis," Dederick said, "Though so far it has not shown signs of generating excesses."
The economy has been growing steadily since the last recession ended in March 1991 and will complete its sixth year of expansion if growth continues into the second quarter.
White House Economic Adviser Alicia Munnell said there were some "one-shot" influences in fourth-quarter GDP, such as a jump in commercial aircraft sales that boosted growth.
She said consumer spending should help the economy continue growing steadily this year.
"The consumer is in remarkably good shape and we expect the consumer to be a major source (of growth) throughout the 1997 period," Munnell said.

Growth in GDP was quite a bit stronger than private economists had anticipated, matching the second-quarter's strong performance. It was the strongest performance since the second quarter of 1994, when GDP grew at a 4.9 percent annual rate.
Stock and bond prices rose after the report, as investors grew convinced that the Fed, the nation's central bank, will hold short-term rates steady at its next policy-setting meeting on Feb. 4-5.

The Dow Jones industrial average added about 19 points to 6,843 and the 30-year Treasury rose nearly a full point, lowering its yield to 6.80 percent from 6.87 percent on Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Two broad measures in the report pointed to minimal inflation. The implicit price deflator rose at a 1.4 percent rate in the quarter, the lowest since 1.3 percent in the first quarter of 1967. And the fixed-weights measure of price changes slowed to a 1.8 percent rate of increase from 2 percent in the third quarter.

Allen Sinai, chief global economist for Primark Decision Economics Inc. in Boston, said he saw no reason for the Fed to act next week but added policy-makers will remain wary about inflation because of the tight job market.
While GDP growth will slow this year, Sinai said, some factors such as consumer spending, brisk commercial construction and strong exports and capital spending will continue, albeit at a slower pace.
"Right now, we have a stronger-than-expected economy with price inflation still contained," Sinai noted. "It's a very pretty picture."

Cold weather and the buoyant stock market played a role in the fourth-quarter jump in activity, the department said, firing up demand at electrical utilities and fattening incomes at brokerages in busy trading.

Consumer spending grew at a $38.8 billion rate in the quarter, up from a $5.9 billion rate the prior quarter. Consumer purchases of goods and services account for two-thirds of economic activity, so the pickup in spending had a big influence on the overall economy.
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced by workers and capital within U.S. borders.
Exports rose at a $47.7 billion rate in the quarter after falling at a $1.8 billion rate. At the same time imports slowed to an $11 billion rate from $20.9 billion.

Separately, the Purchasing Management Association of Chicago said its business barometer index fell to 55.9 in January from 57.1 in December, suggesting a slowdown in industrial activity in the Midwest, though any reading over 50 shows business is growing.
